title: Trump says 'if Ken Paxton loses' Texas Senate race, blame Cornyn and Karl Rove
description: US President Donald Trump speaks in the Rose Garden at the White House, Washington DC, Oct. 15, 2026. Jim Watson | AFP | Getty ImagesPresident Donald
body: US President Donald Trump speaks in the Rose Garden at the White House, Washington DC, Oct. 15, 2026. Jim Watson | AFP | Getty ImagesPresident Donald Trump on Thursday said that if Texas Senate nominee Ken Paxton loses, it will be the fault of incumbent Republican Sen. John Cornyn and conservative commentator Karl Rove.Trump accused Cornyn and Rove of "doing everything possible to make it hard" for Paxton, the state's attorney general, to beat Democratic nominee James Talarico. Cornyn lost the Republican primary to Paxton, whom Trump controversially endorsed."If Ken Paxton loses, it will be because of WEAK and INEFFECTIVE Political Hacks like John Cornyn and Karl Rove, who have ineffectively opposed me for my entire political career," Trump wrote on Truth Social.Trump's preemptive blame-casting came as Texas has surprisingly become one of the most competitive battlegrounds of the 2026 midterm cycle. Most recent polls show state Rep. Talarico maintaining a lead in the low-to-mid single digits over Paxton.The reliably red state has not elected a Democrat to the U.S. Senate since 1988. In 2024, Texans voted for Trump over Democratic presidential nominee Kamala Harris by nearly 14 percentage points.Cornyn's office and Rove did not immediately respond to CNBC's requests for comment on Trump's post.Trump's decision to back Paxton in the GOP primary delivered a major blow to the four-term incumbent Cornyn, whom the president viewed as disloyal. The move was also seen as a major gamble, as Paxton's history of scandal and opposition within his own party has made him a polarizing figure.Hoping to stave off Democrats' goal of winning majority control of the Senate, groups backing Republicans have poured hundreds of millions of dollars into the Texas contest, making it the most expensive race of the cycle.GOP spending in the race has topped $370 million so far, eclipsing Democratic spending by nearly $235 million, according to AdImpact.Trump has repeatedly lashed out at Rove, calling him a "loser" and urging Fox News to stop putting him on air.Rove, who was a senior advisor to former President George W. Bush, "is so bad for the Republican Party, and completely wrong so often," Trump wrote in a Sept. 14 Truth Social post.In a Wall Street Journal op-ed two days later, Rove said that he would back a Democratic candidate in a different race in Texas, voting blue for just the second time in his life.

schema.headline: Trump says 'if Ken Paxton loses' Texas Senate race, blame Cornyn and Karl Rove

title: U.S. reportedly considers use of 'mother of all bombs' as Iran vows to fight on
description: A U.S. Department of Defense (DoD) handout photo shows the Massive Ordinance Air Blast (MOAB) weapon on March 11, 2003 at Eglin Air Force Base, Florid
body: A U.S. Department of Defense (DoD) handout photo shows the Massive Ordinance Air Blast (MOAB) weapon on March 11, 2003 at Eglin Air Force Base, Florida.Usaf | Getty Images News | Getty ImagesThe U.S. military has drawn up options for renewed strikes on Iran that include the potential use of one of the biggest nonnuclear bombs in its arsenal, CNN reported Thursday, as Tehran vowed to continue fighting for its demands. The strike plans involve the possible use of the GBU-43/B Massive Ordnance Air Blast Bomb, nicknamed the "mother of all bombs," CNN reported, citing multiple U.S. officials familiar with the matter. CNBC has not independently confirmed the report. An official told CNBC the Defense Department "plans for a wide range of operational scenarios to execute Presidential and Secretary level direction and to ensure mission success in any operational environment." The 21,600-pound airburst weapon is designed to affect surface targets over a wide area and has so far not been deployed by the U.S. in previous strikes on targets inside Iran. It was used in Afghanistan in 2017 during the previous Trump administration. U.S. President Donald Trump said last week that he would not order a resumption of military strikes before the midterm elections on Nov. 3. Iranian Parliament Speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf said in a televised address late Wednesday that Iran must continue to use a combination of military and defensive capabilities, negotiations, and regional strategic leverage to push the U.S. to accept its demands. Officials in Tehran have previously listed demands including Washington lifting its naval blockade and sanctions and withdrawing U.S. military forces from the region.Ghalibaf said Tehran's goal is not to be locked in an endless war, but to prevent the U.S. and its other adversaries from being able to achieve their own objectives through military attacks, Iranian state-affiliated media reported.

schema.headline: U.S. reportedly considers use of 'mother of all bombs' as Iran vows to fight on

title: Tesla plans next-generation Roadster reveal after almost a decade of delays
description: Tesla CEO Elon Musk during a state dinner in the East Room of the White House in Washington, Sept. 24, 2026.Annabelle Gordon | Bloomberg | Getty Image
body: Tesla CEO Elon Musk during a state dinner in the East Room of the White House in Washington, Sept. 24, 2026.Annabelle Gordon | Bloomberg | Getty ImagesTesla is planning to show off its long-delayed next-generation Roadster on Thursday, almost a decade after Elon Musk's company started taking deposits for the electric sports car. The event will be livestreamed from a SpaceX test site in McGregor, Texas, near Waco. It's expected to begin at 7:55 p.m. local time, or 8:55 p.m. ET.Tesla's original Roadster, designed and engineered by a team led by founding CEO Martin Eberhard, was based on a Lotus Elise chassis and was first delivered in 2008, selling for roughly $100,000 in small volumes until 2012.  The next-generation Roadster is expected to be a high-end, low-volume model that relies on SpaceX technology, such as cold gas thrusters, to enable it to hover. Musk fanatics have been gearing up for the demonstration, expressing their excitement on social media, but the Roadster isn't likely to have any material financial impact on the company.Tesla reopened reservations for the refreshed Roadster in recent weeks, accepting $50,000 deposits from prospective buyers in the U.S., Canada and China. Executives are expected to disclose specific pricing, details and production targets.Musk first promoted the refreshed Roadster concept at an event in November 2017, and the following June in a series of tweets. He wrote at that time, "SpaceX option package for new Tesla Roadster will include ~10 small rocket thrusters arranged seamlessly around car." The engines would improve speed and braking, and may "even allow a Tesla to fly."Tesla started taking $50,000 deposits in 2017, but has since missed every targeted delivery date. As recently as last October, Musk was hyping a Roadster demo that he hoped would happen before the end of 2025. That didn't take place either. Musk's former friend and OpenAI co-founder Sam Altman mocked the Tesla CEO in posts on X last year over the extreme delays, showing screenshots of his own reservation and refund requests. "I really was excited for the car! And I understand delays," Altman wrote. "But 7.5 years has felt like a long time to wait." Altman got his refund, and the two ended up in court earlier this year over a separate matter related to OpenAI's governance and ownership structure. Others have kept their reservations. Lawrence O'Connor, founder and CEO of Other World Computing in Austin, Texas, told CNBC he reserved a Founder's Edition of the new Roadster in November 2017, effectively giving the company what he called an "interest-free loan" of $250,000. O'Connor wrote in a message that he plans to attend Thursday's event and is "excited to see what has been 9 years in the making." According to filings with the Federal Aviation Administration, Tesla established a no-fly zone around the SpaceX facility where it plans to show off the vehicle. The company had to scrap a demo on Oct. 1 due to weather issues. Tesla is scheduled to report third-quarter results after the bell on Wednesday.WATCH: Tesla Roadster unveil set for Thursday evening

schema.headline: Tesla plans next-generation Roadster reveal after almost a decade of delays

title: Wholesale prices jumped 6.3% annually in September, biggest gain since 2022
description: September's producer price index came in much hotter than economists forecast on Thursday, underscoring the continued inflationary pressure from energ
body: September's producer price index came in much hotter than economists forecast on Thursday, underscoring the continued inflationary pressure from energy amid the U.S. war with Iran.The measure of underlying inflation pressures climbed 1.3% in September and 6.3% on an annual basis, according to the Bureau of Labor Statistics. That marked the largest monthly and annual gains since March 2022 and December 2022, respectively.Both readings topped expectations of economists polled by Dow Jones, who forecast an advance of 0.6% on the month and 5.5% annually.Energy drove a sizable chunk of those increases as the Middle East conflict curtailed oil supply and sent prices surging. The so-called core PPI, which excludes volatile food and energy prices from the wholesaler inflation index, added 0.7% on the month and 5% over the 12-month period.But there are signs that soaring energy prices are having downstream effects on other categories. The BLS said in Thursday's release that almost half of September's increase in processed goods for immediate demand was connected to the rise in diesel fuel prices.It's the latest report in recent days showing that inflation continues to hit consumers and companies.Wednesday's consumer price index release showed a rise of 0.6% from August to September and 3.7% on a 12-month basis. Economists polled by Dow Jones had forecast growth of 0.6% and 3.6%, respectively.Excluding food and energy, the core CPI added 0.3% on the month and 2.6% compared with a year ago. Economists anticipated increases of 0.2% and 2.5%, respectively.Wednesday's Beige Book, a chronicle of economic activity published by the Federal Reserve, had the highest number of mentions of terms related to inflation on record, according to an analysis from Bespoke Investment Group.Retail sales grew 0.8% in September, surpassing the rate of 0.4% anticipated by economists, according to government data released in a separate report Thursday. That marked a slowdown from a month prior, when retail sales rose by more than 1%.Excluding spending on autos and gas stations, retail sales increased 0.25% from August to September, a drop from around 1.1% in the prior period. This slowdown offers a sign that high prices related to fuel are causing consumers to tighten the belt elsewhere.This week's data has left a growing minority of fed funds futures traders expecting the central bank to raise rates at its meeting later this month. Traders are now pricing in a nearly 34% likelihood that the Fed hikes borrowing costs on Oct. 28, up from under 18% a week prior, according to CME's FedWatch tool. About 90% expect at least one hike by the end of the year."With a second day in a row of higher-than-expected inflation numbers, it seems the Fed will have no choice but to raise rates again this year," said Chris Zaccarelli, investing chief at Northlight Asset Management.These reports offer some of the final insights into the pace of inflation in the U.S. ahead of the midterm election, which could impact how much power each political party has in Washington.

schema.headline: Wholesale prices jumped 6.3% annually in September, biggest gain since 2022

title: Anthropic taps nonprofits METR and SecureBio to help assess risks and safety practices
description: Dario Amodei, co-founder and chief executive officer of Anthropic, during the World Economic Forum (WEF) in Davos, Switzerland, on Tuesday, Jan. 20, 2
body: Dario Amodei, co-founder and chief executive officer of Anthropic, during the World Economic Forum (WEF) in Davos, Switzerland, on Tuesday, Jan. 20, 2026. Krisztian Bocsi | Bloomberg | Getty ImagesAnthropic on Thursday announced it's working with the nonprofits METR and SecureBio, and engaging in discussions with additional organizations, including Hugging Face, as part of its commitment to embed independent evaluators within the company. The artificial intelligence lab pledged to work closely with third-party evaluators when Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei published his proposal to slow down the pace of model development last month. Amodei said the evaluators would help "verify" Anthropic's adherence to safety practices, and the company selected Accenture to serve as its first partner days later. Independent evaluators like METR, which stands for Model Evaluation and Threat Research, occupied a quiet corner of the multi-trillion-dollar AI industry prior to Amodei's proposal. But as concerns have mounted over whether AI companies can safeguard their models, evaluators have taken on outsized importance. President Donald Trump encouraged AI companies to "partner with an independent external auditor or evaluator" as part of a voluntary accord he presented in late September. Anthropic's Amodei signed the accord, as did top executives at Google, Meta, OpenAI, SpaceX and Nvidia."We're embedding evaluators voluntarily, and we believe every frontier AI company should do the same," Anthropic said Thursday.Read more CNBC tech newsAmazon launches new Bee 'personal AI' devices that listen to conversationsNvidia CEO Jensen Huang urges U.S.-China dialogue on 'potentially dangerous' AIOpenAI sued by 8 states over ChatGPT safety concernsAnthropic's third-quarter revenue is said to hit $16.8 billion ahead of IPOAnthropic is developing three tiers for evaluators that grant varying levels of access to the company and its resources. First-tier evaluators will be able to conduct narrowly scoped risk investigations, second-tier evaluators can publish reports without Anthropic's approval and third-tier evaluators have employee-like access, according to a release. METR is considered a third-tier evaluator, Anthropic said. The company has onboarded six employees from the organization, and they have access to Anthropic hardware, office spaces and tools that are "roughly on par" with what its own risk assessment teams have. The METR employees will analyze Anthropic's risk levels, incidents and practices, and publish their findings. Anthropic is not funding METR's work, according to the company. SecureBio is considered a first-tier evaluator, Anthropic said, so its access is more limited. The organization is reviewing the chemical and biological weapons section of the risk report that it released in August. SecureBio could participate in projects with broader access and publication rights in the future. It's not clear what level of access other organizations like Hugging Face could be granted. Hugging Face is best known for operating an open-source developer platform, and the company was thrust into the spotlight in July, when two of OpenAI's models escaped containment and gained access to Hugging Face systems through the open web. Nvidia acquired Hugging Face for nearly $13 billion last month.  Anthropic said Thursday that it's "working toward an ambitious partnership" with Accenture, but it didn't disclose how that company fits into its tiered system. Anthropic said last month that it would fund Accenture's work directly "given the importance and urgency of this work," prompting critics to raise concerns about its independence on social media. "There are, as yet, no standards for what information embedded evaluators should have access to, or how they should report what they find. There is also no settled system for funding independent evaluation," Anthropic said in a release at the time. "Long-term, we think funding should come from pooled or government sources, as we called for in our Advanced AI Framework in June. As neither exists today, we plan to work with different evaluators under different funding arrangements."WATCH: Our data continues to show Anthropic’s gaining market share, not losing: Menlo Ventures’ Matt Murphywatch now

title: The problem with 'good debt': Why borrowers should think twice about the label
description: watch nowWhen Bryanna Hambrick bought a three-bedroom, two-bathroom single-family home in Columbus, Ohio, in 2022, she hoped that life milestone would
body: watch nowWhen Bryanna Hambrick bought a three-bedroom, two-bathroom single-family home in Columbus, Ohio, in 2022, she hoped that life milestone would help her save money on rent and build wealth."Society puts a lot of pressure on you to have property, get married, have kids," said the 35-year-old. "Life wasn't giving me those other things, so I was like, well, I can buy a home. I can control that."But her purchase came with a monthly payment of nearly $1,200, about $200 more than expected, after a property tax reassessment and a higher-than-anticipated interest rate on her mortgage. Much of her savings went toward closing costs, Hambrick said, while expensive and unexpected home repairs have kept her living paycheck to paycheck in the years since."Anytime I've gotten a certain dollar amount in my savings that makes me feel a little bit more comfortable, something happens," Hambrick said.Hambrick's experience highlights what experts say is a broader problem: Even debt that seems like a sound investment can become a financial burden.Read more CNBC 'Good Debt' coverageThe problem with 'good debt': Why borrowers should think twice about the labelCollege was supposed to be a smart investment — until it got risky. How we got hereWhy college and homeownership don't feel worth it anymoreShe graduated with manageable student debt. Can her daughters do the same?Who gets to have 'good' debt? A sociologist, theologian and philosopher weigh inMortgages and student loans are often called "good debt" because they may help borrowers build wealth or increase their earning power. "Bad debt," by contrast, often includes credit card balances as well as auto and personal loans, because they often finance consumption or assets that can lose value.But financial experts say the "good debt" label can downplay the risk for borrowers and lead them to overextend themselves, making repayment challenging."I try to avoid talking about 'good debt' now," said Sheila Bair, an author and advisor who chaired the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation from 2006 to 2011. "I think your presumption should always be against debt ... it's a burden on your financial future, and there are a lot of ways it's marketed that make it look like it's not."  Look beyond the 'good debt' labelDavid Plunkert | CNBCEven if a purchase seems to check all the boxes, you need to consider the long term. "Young people shouldn't feel pressured to buy a home or borrow to go to college," said Bair, a member of the CNBC Global Financial Wellness Advisory Board and former president of Washington College. "It's a decision that needs to make sense for you financially, and for some people, it won't."She recommends asking yourself whether taking on debt will improve your financial well-being. Then dig into the details.For example, whether a mortgage is financially sound depends on factors including the home price, loan terms, and the borrower's income stability and financial reserves.  Experts say you should do your own calculations to figure out how much mortgage payment you feel comfortable with. Don't expect lenders to tell you how much house you can afford; mortgage companies consider what you can repay, not what's in your budget.  "Make sure your mortgage is affordable before you do anything else, and make sure you're going to be there for many years, because home prices over time will appreciate in value, but they go up and down," said Bair. She recommends planning to live in the home for at least five years to account for transaction costs and the possibility of short-term price declines. The housing crash that precipitated the 2008 financial crisis shows how debt commonly viewed as "good" can go bad. Average U.S. home prices rose sharply between 1998 and 2006 as mortgage lending expanded, including to borrowers with weaker credit. Some borrowers took on large mortgages, betting that home values would keep rising. "A lot of the folks that had those subprime mortgages didn't understand what they were getting," said Bair. When home prices fell and payments rose on some adjustable-rate mortgages, foreclosures surged. There were about 3.8 million foreclosures between 2007 and 2010, according to an analysis by the Federal Reserve Bank of Chicago.Why even 'good' debt can become a mistakeBeyond the fundamentals such as interest rates and repayment terms, borrowers should examine their motivations and expectations before taking on debt, said Brad Klontz, a financial psychologist and certified financial planner.Many people get tripped up by impulse borrowing, tying self-worth to big purchases, and too-rosy expectations about future earnings, he said."We have some chronic debt mistakes that we're all vulnerable to," said Klontz, who is a member of the CNBC Financial Advisor Council and the CNBC Global Financial Wellness Advisory Board.He recommends people approach debt as a business decision — and temper their expectations. If, say, buying a home or getting a master's degree has the potential to generate wealth, don't automatically assume it will; consider the risk and return on that investment, he said.Make sure your assumptions aren't overly optimistic. For example, when considering education spending, research potential careers and salaries in the government's Occupational Outlook Handbook. Then work backward and ask: "Does it make sense for me to take on student loan debt to get a degree? Do you even need a degree?" Klontz said.Avoid emotional borrowing to fund a lifestyle, impress others, or pay for short-term experiences, said Klontz."If you're taking on debt to travel, that is a financial mistake," Klontz said. Instead, he suggests planning and saving for travel experiences.  "A lot of times, when people are overspending or taking on debt for a vacation, it's somewhat of an impulse purchase." That can lead to long-term regret, he said, "because you're having that emotional experience, and then you come back home to reality, and now you're stuck with the chronic stress of trying to pay that off."Klontz said one of the biggest mistakes he sees people make is buying the "absolute biggest, best house [they] can possibly afford." "Even people who are really wise with money fall into that mistake," Klontz said. They may overestimate their ability to make more money in the future and underestimate how much they will spend on repairs and maintenance, he said. Bryanna Hambrick after buying her first home.Courtesy: Bryanna HambrickHambrick said she wishes she had focused more on the cost of the home than the hardwood floors and granite countertops. "Your first house doesn't have to be your forever home," she said. Hambrick's home value has appreciated, but not as much as she expected. "It feels like bad debt, bad decision overall," she said.  — CNBC's Nathaniel Lee contributed reporting.

schema.headline: The problem with 'good debt': Why borrowers should think twice about the label

title: Harvard’s endowment jumps 27% in fiscal 2026, lifted by SpaceX as top holding
description: Students walk on campus at Harvard University, in Cambridge, Massachusetts, Nov. 19, 2025.Reba Saldanha | ReutersHarvard University's endowment grew 2
body: Students walk on campus at Harvard University, in Cambridge, Massachusetts, Nov. 19, 2025.Reba Saldanha | ReutersHarvard University's endowment grew 27.1% in fiscal year 2026, its strongest return in five years, the school said in its annual financial report released on Thursday. The endowment, which beat the S&P 500's 22.3% total return in the same period by 4.8 percentage points, now totals nearly $68 billion. The outperformance came amid actions by the Trump administration to penalize the school and withhold funding from the university. "While markets can easily take back what they give, that return will strengthen the endowment's capacity to support the University over time," Harvard's chief financial officer Ritu Kalra and treasurer Timothy Barakett wrote in the 49-page annual report. "The University deliberately smooths distributions so that operating support does not rise and fall with the markets. Strong investment returns therefore support Harvard's work gradually, through future distributions."The returns marked the best year for the endowment, managed by the Harvard Management Company, since 2021. Harvard's fiscal year ends on June 30. In its second-quarter 13F filing with the Securities and Exchange Commission, Harvard unveiled a $2.2 billion stake in Elon Musk's SpaceX rocket and satellite company. It marked the endowment's largest single holding by value, trailed by Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company at just under $350 million. Harvard's financial picture, though, is undermined by moves by the federal government. Federally-sponsored research revenue declined 19.5% to $509 million in fiscal 2026. And starting in the current fiscal year, "endowment resources will face an additional constraint, with the federal excise tax on Harvard's net investment income rising nearly six-fold, from 1.4% to 8%," Kalra and Barakett wrote. "We estimate the higher rate will cost roughly $300 million a year.""[I]n a year of returns like this one," the federal excise tax "would be several times larger," they noted.President Alan Garber acknowledged such headwinds, but said in the report that Harvard can still succeed."Together, we have the opportunity to set the University on a path to excellence that none of us can imagine today," he said. "Notwithstanding the challenges and uncertainty, this is a thrilling time to be part of a great American institution devoted to Veritas."

schema.headline: Harvard’s endowment jumps 27% in fiscal 2026, lifted by SpaceX as top holding

title: Nvidia, AMD, Dell sink in global tech rout on AI funding worries
description: watch nowStocks tied to the artificial intelligence trade sank on Thursday, continuing a global sell-off.Collectively, 20 of the most valuable global
body: watch nowStocks tied to the artificial intelligence trade sank on Thursday, continuing a global sell-off.Collectively, 20 of the most valuable global AI and semiconductor stocks have shed more than $1 trillion in value so far this week, as interest rate hikes, AI financing and intensifying competition weighed on sentiment.Nvidia lost 1.84% while AMD sank 1.5% and Intel lost about 2.8%. Dell Technologies sank 6.8%. Micron shares whipsawed and closed 1.87% higher.Neoclouds started the day in the dumps on Thursday, but recovered, with CoreWeave closing 5.94% higher and Nebius adding 1.29%. IREN finished the day down marginally.Shares in the neoclouds rebounded after comments from Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang seemed to settle fears in the AI trade.Huang told Bloomberg at an event in Stockholm, Sweden, that he didn't see a need for Nvidia to backstop CoreWeave and that, "Their cost of capital is actually decreasing." A sell-off in global technology hardware stocks also deepened across Asia and Europe on Thursday.South Korean chip giant SK Hynix plunged more than 10%, while rival Samsung Electronics fell 8.73%. Other South Korean chip-related stocks also came under pressure. LG Innotek sank 8.95%, Seoul Semiconductor shed 9.28% and Samsung SDI declined 6.26%.In Japan, technology investment giant SoftBank Group tumbled 7.9%. Semiconductor testing equipment maker Advantest plunged almost 14%, while chipmaking equipment supplier Tokyo Electron lost 6.45%. Renesas Electronics declined 8%. Taiwan's TSMC, the world's largest contract chipmaker, fell 1.81%.Over in Europe, Dutch semiconductor giant ASML traded marginally lower, Infineon Technologies shed 5% and ASM International was down 7%.Stock Chart IconStock chart iconCoreWeave, Nebius and IREN stock chart.Why stocks are selling offThe declines come as investors grow increasingly concerned that higher borrowing costs could weigh on the massive capital spending required to build out AI infrastructure, putting pressure on technology companies that have benefited from the AI investment boom.Concerns around global memory chip oversupply as early as 2029, as manufacturers ramp up production capacity to meet surging demand from artificial intelligence, also seem to be weighing down sentiment. China's ChangXin Memory Technologies, or CXMT, said over the weekend that it had made a breakthrough on a new architecture that could boost memory density by packing more data into a smaller space, signaling intensifying competition in the memory space. Elon Musk in an X post said China would be making "a LOT of RAM in 2028."  Chief executives of Broadcom and Intel, meanwhile, warned on Monday that financing could become a major headwind to the AI boom, with Broadcom's Hock Tan saying it could be bigger challenge to AI expansion than shortages of chips or electricity. The sell-off followed a bruising session on Wall Street Wednesday, where technology shares led broader market losses after hotter-than-expected U.S. inflation data fueled concerns that the Federal Reserve could raise interest rates further.The tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite dropped 1.88% to close at 26,692.87, while the S&P 500 shed 1.11% to end at 7,718.94. The Dow Jones Industrial Average slipped 0.09%.watch nowDan Ives, tech analyst at Yorkville Ives, said the latest sell-off in AI-related stocks reflects growing concerns over the cost of financing massive infrastructure projects as U.S. Treasury yields climb above 5%, but added that underlying demand for AI computing power remains robust."Higher yields raise the cost of financing these builds, and investors are right to focus on balance sheets and contract structure, but rates are a financing question, not a demand question," Ives said in a note.The latest pullback presents a buying opportunity, Ives said, adding that the AI infrastructure boom remained in its early stages despite mounting concerns over funding costs. "What would change our view is a demand signal, not a rate signal," he said, pointing to potential cuts in hyperscaler capital expenditure plans, canceled contracts or falling GPU rental prices as warning signs.Read more CNBC tech newsAmazon launches new Bee 'personal AI' devices that listen to conversationsNvidia CEO Jensen Huang urges U.S.-China dialogue on 'potentially dangerous' AIOpenAI sued by 8 states over ChatGPT safety concernsAnthropic's third-quarter revenue is said to hit $16.8 billion ahead of IPO

title: She made college ‘good debt’ for herself. Can she do the same for her daughter?
description: watch nowWhen Stephanie Thomas went to college more than 25 years ago, she relied on some financial help from her parents, student loans and a part-ti
body: watch nowWhen Stephanie Thomas went to college more than 25 years ago, she relied on some financial help from her parents, student loans and a part-time job as a gymnastics coach to cover most of the tab. Even so, by graduation she had amassed about $20,000 in student loans — "good debt" she was manageably able to pay off over the years on an income-based repayment plan. But when it came to her daughters' education, Thomas, now 49 and a certified financial planner in Raleigh, North Carolina, knew her family would need to work harder to limit student debt and boost the return on investment for a college degree. She and her husband saved diligently in 529 college savings plans and, as their daughters approached college age, looked for other ways to cut costs. Thomas' youngest daughter, Ainsley, 16, is taking college-level coursework in high school through dual enrollment. By the time she receives her diploma, she'll also have a two-year associate's degree and enough credits to start a four-year institution as a junior. It's a tactic more students are utilizing to shave years off the price of a bachelor's degree, according to the latest spring 2026 report from the National Student Clearinghouse Research Center, which showed a 9.6% jump in dual enrollment from the previous year. Stephanie Thomas and her daughter Ainsley.Justin Kase Conder | CNBCThere's good reason families are increasingly keen to cut college costs. Between 1995 and 2025, average tuition and fees rose 74% at private four-year institutions and 101% at four-year public colleges, after adjusting for inflation, according to the College Board, a nonprofit organization that tracks trends in college pricing and student aid."We're trying to be strategic about reducing the overall cost," Thomas said. "With the rising cost of higher education, finding creative ways to cut expenses feels much more practical."Asking the question: Is college 'worth what it costs'?A generation ago, it was much more common to do as Thomas did, but today self-funding an education with some financial aid and a part-time job has become far less feasible, experts say. Not only has the price of college significantly increased, but concerns have also grown about taking on the student loan debt needed to cover the tab. Now, nearly half of families borrow money to pay for college, according to private lender Sallie's recent How America Pays for College report, pushing outstanding student debt to a stunning $1.85 trillion, including federal and private loans.Read more CNBC 'Good Debt' coverageThe problem with 'good debt': Why borrowers should think twice about the labelCollege was supposed to be a smart investment — until it got risky. How we got hereWhy college and homeownership don't feel worth it anymoreShe graduated with manageable student debt. Can her daughters do the same?Who gets to have 'good' debt? A sociologist, theologian and philosopher weigh inDuring the Great Recession, deep cuts in state funding helped drive sharp tuition increases, shifting the costs to students, according to the Center on Budget and Policy Priorities, a nonpartisan research group based in Washington, D.C. The brief recession sparked by the Covid pandemic triggered another wave of funding cuts for colleges and universities. By the 2025-26 academic year, room and board, tuition, and fees reached $25,850 at four-year, in-state public colleges, and $45,780 for out-of-state students, on average, according to the College Board. At four-year private colleges, it costs $60,920 annually.A college education is now one of the largest investments an individual will make in their lifetime.David Plunkert | CNBCThe burden on students increased as college tuition and other expenses hit record highs. These days, parent income and savings cover less than half of college costs, at 39%, while student income and savings represent 10%, Sallie's report also found. Free money from scholarships and grants accounts for about 27% of the costs, and student loans, including parent borrowing, make up most of the rest.That debt load has become more difficult to manage: As of June 30, about 9.3 million federal student loan borrowers were in default, up from around 6.2 million at the same time in 2016, according to Education Department data released last month. That's a roughly 50% increase over the last decade.Rising debt levels among graduates is part of the reason behind recent efforts by the Trump administration to curb access to federal loans, including implementing a total lifetime borrowing limit, to provide a check on soaring tuition costs.Assessing the affordability of a degreeThen, there's the question of the return on investment. Taking on debt, for instance, becomes far more palatable when the payments are affordable — and that can't happen without first being able to get a good job with a decent salary.But the future of early-career employment is increasingly ambiguous, largely due to the rapid rise of artificial intelligence, according to the National Association of Colleges and Employers. Postings for entry-level positions in the U.S. sank 35% since January 2023, labor research firm Revelio Labs found, with AI playing a big role.Jobs in technology and software development, for example, are under pressure, according to a separate report by job site Indeed. Alternatively, home health and nursing roles are more insulated, the report found. Given an uncertain job market, families are questioning the value of college, and some students are forgoing a four-year degree altogether. Many are looking at alternative pathways and short-term programs, other research by the National Student Clearinghouse Research Center shows.Enrollments in undergraduate certificate and associate degree programs both grew by about 2% last year, while enrollment in bachelor's degree programs rose by less than 1%, the research found. Community colleges now enroll 752,000 students in undergraduate certificate programs — a 28% jump from just four years ago.Staying positive: 'Americans haven't given up on higher education'Most parents of children under age 18 want their child to pursue some form of education immediately after high school — and ideally, a bachelor's degree, a recent Lumina Foundation and Gallup poll found. Indeed, a four-year degree is still seen as the "gold standard," according to Courtney Brown, chief data and research officer for the Lumina Foundation, which is focused on advancing higher education opportunities. Even with the rise of AI, a college degree is widely viewed as the best pathway to upward mobility — particularly in tight job markets.Stephanie Thomas’ daughter, Ainsley, 16.Justin Kase Conder | CNBCUltimately, it's just less of a sure thing. "Americans haven't given up on higher education. They want it for their children … but they are questioning whether they can afford it," Brown said. The question is not whether college is worth the investment, she added, "but is it worth what it costs?" For Thomas and her daughter, the calculus of finishing sooner is just too compelling. When Ainsley completes her associate's degree, she wants to attend North Carolina State University, a public college in Raleigh, for another two years. If all goes according to plan, she'll get her bachelor's degree in 2030. But by then, the family anticipates, she'll have cut the tab in half — and her borrowing costs to near zero. Subscribe to CNBC on YouTube.

schema.headline: She made college ‘good debt’ for herself. Can she do the same for her daughter?

title: KFC to switch to Coca-Cola beverages in U.S. restaurants for the first time in decades
description: A view of a KFC restaurant in Vallejo, California.Justin Sullivan | Getty ImagesKFC's U.S. restaurants will ditch PepsiCo and switch to Coca-Cola beve
body: A view of a KFC restaurant in Vallejo, California.Justin Sullivan | Getty ImagesKFC's U.S. restaurants will ditch PepsiCo and switch to Coca-Cola beverages next year, marking the first time in decades that the Yum Brands chain has changed its drink supplier, the restaurant company said Thursday.Some of KFC's international markets serve Coke products, but the chain's U.S. restaurants have stuck with PepsiCo drinks ever since Pepsi bought KFC in 1986. At the time of the acquisition, KFC was Coke's second-largest fountain account, trailing only McDonald's. Pepsi later spun off KFC, along with sister chains Pizza Hut and Taco Bell — but even as the combined Yum Brands, the company stayed loyal to its previous owner. Without Pepsi, Taco Bell would not serve its iconic Mountain Dew Baja Blast.The change comes as KFC aims to win back U.S. diners, who have ditched the fried chicken chain for rivals such as Chick-fil-A or Popeyes. "This decision is a critical step in the Kentucky Fried Comeback," KFC U.S. President Catherine Tan-Gillespie wrote in a memo to franchisees and employees obtained by CNBC. "A new beverage offering, with a new partner in Coca-Cola, gives us a platform to innovate, meet changing tastes and give customers more reasons to choose us."Beverage cups stacked inside a Yum Brands KFC restaurant in Shelbyville, Kentucky, Jan. 29, 2021.Luke Sharrett | Bloomberg | Getty ImagesFor many fast-food chains, beverages have become a critical way to attract consumers. A number of restaurants, including McDonald's and Taco Bell, have broadened their drink offerings with options such as refreshers or "dirty soda." For its part, KFC recently unveiled new drinks, including iced coffees and shakes, at Open House, its innovation restaurant in McKinney, Texas. Coke told CNBC earlier this year that the company has helped many of its restaurant partners create new drinks.KFC expects to be pouring Coke beverages in all of its U.S. restaurants by the end of the first quarter of 2027, Tan-Gillespie said.Tan-Gillespie also said that Pepsi remains an important partner for KFC's parent company and the chain's international markets.For decades, Coke and Pepsi have tussled over important restaurant partners, which represent both a sales opportunity and the chance to grow the visibility of their beverage brands. It is unusual for large restaurant chains to switch beverage providers, but not unprecedented. In 2024, Pepsi poached Subway, the largest U.S. restaurant chain by number of locations, from Coke. Besides KFC, Coke has wooed away a number of notable Pepsi customers in recent years, including Culver's, Arby's and Panda Express.

schema.headline: KFC to switch to Coca-Cola beverages in U.S. restaurants for the first time in decades

title: Some 'classic' money advice is actually pretty new—and not all of it is worthwhile, says historian
description: In the world of personal finance, many of the lessons we're taught are touted as historical. Since the dawn of time, the experts tell us, those who go
body: In the world of personal finance, many of the lessons we're taught are touted as historical. Since the dawn of time, the experts tell us, those who got ahead financially lived within their means, saved diligently and spent and invested carefully.It made Joseph Moore — a historian and author of "How to Get Rich in American History," published in April — wonder if Americans had been receiving, following and prospering from the same advice for the past few centuries. What he found surprised him."Is there timeless wisdom of money that we should all be following, from Ben Franklin to now? The answer is no," Moore says. "It turns out, what 'always' worked is always changing."Some common financial principles that seem old are recent phenomena, Moore says, and some situations that seem new are, in fact, quite common throughout history.In both such cases, knowing your history can be helpful. After all, if previous generations flourished without more recent advice, maybe the current wisdom isn't as valuable as we think. Conversely, maybe you don't need to find a creative solution to a problem that isn't actually that novel.Here are three misconceptions Moore points out from the history of American personal finance — and what you can learn from them.Housing shortages aren't newAmericans are struggling with housing affordability amid high mortgage rates and rising home prices. But it's not a historically unique problem, Moore says."We absolutely are in a housing crisis caused by a housing shortage," he says. "It's neither the first nor the worst."Moore points to 1948, when the ratio of people who wanted to buy a house to available inventory was about double what it is now, as the worst culprit. The year 1981, when the median new mortgage consumed more than half of the median household income, was no picnic either, he says.That doesn't mean that the current shortage isn't real or that you should suck it up because other people had it worse, Moore says. But it is worth looking at how people have historically solved it — personally, not politically. And in the case of a housing shortage, Moore's answers aren't glamorous. One historical solution was moving more often. Currently, the housing market is worse in some places than others. Folks used to be more likely to pick up and go to places where opportunities were better, Moore says. For most of the country's history, between 1 in 3 and 1 in 5 Americans moved every year, he says, pointing to research by historian and journalist Yoni Appelbaum. Now, it's more like 1 in 13, Moore notes.Another common solution for unaffordable homes: sharing housing. In 19th-century America, it wasn't at all uncommon for homeowners to rent out rooms in their house to help with the mortgage, Moore says. The same logic applies to modern-day renters who split spaces with roommates to keep costs down, he says."It's a shortage of space, so you have to monetize space," says Moore.Diversification and compounding weren't the historical path to wealthInvestors are often told that the path to long-term wealth is simple: Invest consistently in a low-cost, broadly diversified stock portfolio. Need proof? Consider the S&P 500's upward trajectory since before the stock market crash in 1929, and think of all the compounding returns you could have earned over that period had you invested."Something really new that we act like is really old is that compound interest is what builds wealth," Moore says. "Nobody got rich by compound interest for most of U.S. history, and if they did, they were generally already wealthy."Think about it: Index funds weren't around, nor were fractional shares. If you wanted to own every stock in an index, you'd need to have the money to buy shares of each, plus a fee for your broker, of course. "For most of American history, less than 10% of Americans owned stocks at all. That's not how people got wealthy," Moore says. "They got wealthy by concentrating most of their efforts in small businesses and careers, real estate and job tools. [Few people] compounded their way to wealth until the greatest generation and baby boomers, when the technology came online to allow you to use compounding."Investors should still take advantage of the innovations that made diversified, low-cost portfolios widely accessible, Moore says. Just remember that there's more than one way to build wealth.People used to keep budgeting simpleOne piece of financial advice that feels tried and true is to create a budget and stick to it. How else can you make sure you don't overspend and keep yourself on track toward your financial goals?But Moore says that the household spending spreadsheet is a relatively new phenomenon."Nobody in the 1800s budgeted the way we talk about budgeting," he says. "These forward-facing spending categories would be completely foreign to anyone's thinking."For most of American history, what folks did instead was look at their money in big buckets. A couple might divide things between the husband's and wife's income, for instance, he says. Or, to keep things even simpler, they divided income between what they needed to survive, and whatever was leftover. More complex budgeting schemes came into fashion in the early 20th century, Moore says, with financial guides at the time touting how much you could save by slashing the likes of alcohol and tobacco — the lattes and avocado toast of their day.There's no one right way to manage money. But if you find budgeting tedious, Moore argues that attitude puts you in line with generations of Americans who kept things simple by practicing what we'd now call reverse budgeting: paying their bills, putting money away for goals and then spending the rest as they saw fit.

schema.headline: Some 'classic' money advice is actually pretty new—and not all of it is worthwhile, says historian

title: JetBlue’s new domestic first class, BlueFirst, is now on sale
description: A JetBlue Airbus A321 lands at Los Angeles International Airport on March 7, 2026 in Los Angeles, California. Kevin Carter | Getty ImagesJetBlue's new
body: A JetBlue Airbus A321 lands at Los Angeles International Airport on March 7, 2026 in Los Angeles, California. Kevin Carter | Getty ImagesJetBlue's new domestic first class, BlueFirst, is now available for booking on flights across more than 30 routes, the airline said Thursday.This option will be available on domestic flights that are not currently served by the airline's lie-flat Mint business class, which it offers on longer flights. It's part of an overhaul of the carrier's fare options, which will include basic options that don't come with things like seat assignments, a standard option, and a "flex" option, which is refundable and more easily changed.The new first-class section comes as JetBlue seeks to return to steady profitability by growing its higher-priced offerings amid strong demand for more expensive and roomier seats.The first flight with BlueFirst seats will be on Dec. 8, between Boston and Fort Lauderdale, Florida, followed by routes between Fort Lauderdale and New York's LaGuardia Airport, with additional flights being rolled out in the following weeks and months. JetBlue is offering some introductory fares for BlueFirst seats for select flights, including a $299 flight from Boston to Fort Lauderdale, a $249 option from New York to Fort Lauderdale and a $299 option from New York to Liberia, Costa Rica. The first-class tickets will offer seats that recline up to 5 inches and have up to 7 inches more legroom than Main seats, JetBlue said. Other perks include Bluetooth-connected seatback screens, food and beverage options, Group 1 boarding and expedited security.  Within the BlueFirst class, there are three tiered fare options:  BlueFirst Base, a lower-cost option, includes one checked bag, priority check-in and security, and Group 1 boarding. Seat selection is free within 24 hours of departure, but there are fees for changes and cancellations.BlueFirst includes two checked bags, free seat selection, and no change or cancellation fees. BlueFirst Flex has the same perks as BlueFirst and additionally offers refunds if you cancel your flight ahead of the departure, with no fees for same-day switches or standby.   "We designed BlueFirst to deliver a more accessible first-class experience that combines the thoughtful hospitality and service customers expect from JetBlue with exceptional value and comfort. We're excited that customers can now start making BlueFirst part of their travel plans," JetBlue CEO Joanna Geraghty said in a news release.

schema.headline: JetBlue’s new domestic first class, BlueFirst, is now on sale

title: U.S. sues California in fight over checking citizenship of mail voters
description: A voter drops a mail-in ballot at an official drop box inside City Hall during a primary election in San Francisco, California, on Tuesday, June 2, 20
body: A voter drops a mail-in ballot at an official drop box inside City Hall during a primary election in San Francisco, California, on Tuesday, June 2, 2026.David Paul Morris | Bloomberg | Getty ImagesThe federal government sued the state of California on Thursday in an escalating battle over how to prevent non-U.S. citizens from voting by mail in federal elections.The  lawsuit is the latest action by the Department of Justice targeting state administration of elections, which President Donald Trump has often criticized as susceptible to fraud and voting by noncitizens.The civil complaint, which the DOJ had threatened to file, asks a judge to prevent California officials from tabulating mail-in ballots "from likely non-citizens in the upcoming federal election until the voter's citizenship status can be determined."The Department of Justice asks that a judge order the state to set aside mail ballots from voters "identified by the Federal Government likely to be noncitizens," and to verify their citizenship status before their ballot is counted.Non-citizens are barred from voting in federal elections. California Gov. Gavin Newsom, in a post on X on Wednesday, said, in anticipation of the suit, "More dangerous nonsense from a President losing his grip on reality.""Trump is now demanding that California election officials VIOLATE federal law," Newsom wrote. "Apparently, the rule of law only matters when it's convenient for MAGA's dear leader. California's elections are NOT Donald Trump's to control. We will ensure EVERY California voter can participate in a free and fair election.The suit in U.S. District Court in Los Angeles came two days after acting U.S. Deputy Attorney General Trent McCotter, in a letter to California Secretary of State Shirley Weber, gave the state 48 hours to determine whether any U.S. citizens were on a list of people the DOJ believes are likely noncitizens who were sent ballots for the Nov. 3 election.The DOJ previously gave officials in Los Angeles County a thumb drive containing the questioned names to officials in Los Angeles County. McCotter told Weber the state needed to tell local election officials to segregate mail ballots until the citizenship status of their voters could be determined, and not send a ballot to anyone who had not yet received one."If you cannot implement this process by then, given the ongoing federal election, the United States will have no choice but to seek emergency relief," McCotter said in his letter.Weber's office, in a statement on Thursday, said, "In July of this year, President Trump and DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullen made (still) unsubstantiated claims that California had 190,000 non-citizens on its voter rolls.""Given the many high-profile examples of states purging US citizens from their voter rolls based on DHS/SAVE data, SOS immediately requested written information about their methodology and data sources to back up their claims," Weber's office said. "They refused and provided California with nothing.""Now the USDOJ, under threat of 'emergency' litigation, demands that California blindly trust this administration without any evidence or legal authority to justify its request."Weber, in a statement Thursday, said the DOJ's "relentless efforts to unlawfully gain access to states' protected voter data and purge voter rolls serve only to cause chaos and fuel public distrust in our elections."She also said that California "has robust state law requirements that only U.S. citizens can register to vote and that any non-eligible registrants are removed from the State's voter rolls.""My office and California election officials remain committed – as always – to ensuring a fair and smooth 2026 General Election," Weber said.Weber's office declined to comment on the lawsuit Thursday, but pointed to a letter she had sent McCotter in response to his letter.Weber, in her letter, said, "California's election administration will continue to be governed by applicable federal and state law, not by unsubstantiated claims and outrageous demands."She said that "despite failing to send the list of alleged non-citizens to my office, you demand that we request transmittal of the list, review and confirm the citizenship status of each of the approximately 20,000 individuals on the list on the eve of an election and within a mere 48 hours.""This is an emergency of the DOJ's creation," Weber said.

schema.headline: U.S. sues California in fight over checking citizenship of mail voters

title: Porsche reveals Mission S concept car that previews new design identity
description: The Porsche Mission S concept car.Courtesy PorschePorsche on Thursday revealed a concept car called Mission S that signals a new design direction and
body: The Porsche Mission S concept car.Courtesy PorschePorsche on Thursday revealed a concept car called Mission S that signals a new design direction and flagship model for the famed German sports carmaker.The debut of the sleek midengine vehicle is part of a turnaround plan revealed last week by the Volkswagen-controlled brand that includes efforts to boost profits through higher-end products and lower vehicle sales.Porsche described Mission S as "a first glimpse of the brand's evolved design identity" that also represents a "super sports car platform" that will be positioned above its iconic 911 sports car.The vehicle's design is recognizably Porsche but with more aggressive styling compared with its current models, including new hood vents and a roof scoop. Its rear features more differentiated flair in which the vehicle's spoiler flows into its rear panels.The rear of the Porsche Mission S concept car.Courtesy Porsche"A Porsche must be recognisable as a Porsche at first glance," Porsche Chairman Michael Leiters said in a release. "The Mission S provides a glimpse of the ideas and design features that will shape Porsche in the coming years."Automakers routinely use concept vehicles to gauge customer interest, showcase future technologies and signal the direction of a vehicle or brand.The company did not release expected pricing or performance specifications for such future models. Starting prices for its current 911 models range from roughly $135,500 for an entry-level Carrera to more than $203,000 for a Carrera 4 GTS convertible.The interior of the Porsche Mission S concept car.Courtesy PorscheDuring Porsche's capital markets day on Oct. 7, the company outlined its "Sportwagenschmiede '35" turnaround plan, which focuses on emphasizing high-end sports cars and luxury SUVs to get the carmaker back on track. Porsche's operating margin last year was only 1.1%, compared with 14.1% in 2024, as the company deals with increased costs, U.S. tariffs and declining sales in China.The turnaround plan includes a long-term target for a group ‌operating margin of 15% and a midterm breakeven point of 200,000 units or below annually. That compares with sales of 279,449 in 2025.

schema.headline: Porsche reveals Mission S concept car that previews new design identity

title: Democrat Talarico says he raised record $64 million over summer in Texas Senate race
description: Democratic U.S. Senate candidate James Talarico speaks during a “Talarico for Texas: Frontera Tour” campaign rally at the International Center For Tra
body: Democratic U.S. Senate candidate James Talarico speaks during a “Talarico for Texas: Frontera Tour” campaign rally at the International Center For Trade convention center on July 13, 2026 in Eagle Pass, Texas. Brandon Bell | Getty ImagesDemocratic Texas Senate candidate James Talarico raised $64 million in the third quarter, his campaign announced Thursday, setting what the campaign said is a Senate fundraising record as Republicans pour outside money into the race to bolster GOP nominee Ken Paxton in the 2026 midterm election.The haul was the largest ever reported by a Senate candidate in the July-through-September quarter, according to the campaign, surpassing the previous record of $57 million set by South Carolina Democrat Jaime Harrison, who unsuccessfully ran against Republican Lindsey Graham in 2020.Talarico has raised more than $134 million since launching his campaign last year, according to his campaign ahead of the quarterly filing deadline with the Federal Election Commission.“Grassroots contributors from across Texas are coming together to end billionaire control over our politics and bring down costs for working families,” Talarico said in a statement.The campaign said more than 1.3 million people have donated and that 97% of contributions were $100 or less. Paxton, by comparison, announced earlier this month that his campaign and two affiliated fundraising committees raised a combined $18 million during the quarter.The candidates' full financial picture will become clearer after their quarterly reports are filed with the FEC. The filings will show how much each campaign spent and how much cash they had left entering the final stretch.But the gap in direct fundraising tells only part of the financial story. Republican outside groups have spent more than $175 million since Sept. 1 supporting Paxton or attacking Talarico, according to AdImpact, helping offset Paxton's weaker campaign fundraising. Overall political advertising in the race has surpassed $500 million.SpaceX and Tesla CEO Elon Musk has emerged as a major force in the race, giving $10 million to a pro-Paxton super PAC, according to figures confirmed Monday by a spokesman for Musk's America PAC,  while his America PAC has spent about $9.4 million attacking Talarico and another $1.8 million supporting Paxton, according to FEC filings.   The source of that money matters as federal law guarantees candidates lower broadcast rates for television advertising than super PACs, allowing Talarico's campaign dollars to go further in buying TV exposure than outside Republican groups.No Democrat has won statewide in Texas since 1994, and the party has not won a U.S. Senate race there since 1988. But Talarico leads Paxton 48.5% to 45.2% in FiftyPlusOne's polling average, a 3.3-percentage point advantage, forcing Republicans to devote significant resources to what has traditionally been safe territory.Talarico's fundraising also eclipses previous high-water marks for Texas Democrats. Beto O'Rourke raised $38.1 million in the third quarter of 2018 during his challenge to Republican Sen. Ted Cruz.

schema.headline: Democrat Talarico says he raised record $64 million over summer in Texas Senate race
